move.title: A roux filling under a butter crust
move.body: Chicken pot pie is chicken and vegetables in a creamy sauce, baked under a golden crust. Today you'll make the pastry, cook the chicken, thicken broth and milk with a roux, and bake the filling under a crust in the same skillet.

callback.body: The quiche taught you a butter crust under a filling. Here the same crust goes on top, so it bakes crisp in the dry oven heat, with vents to let the steam out.

why.title: Cold butter, flaky crust
why.body: Pieces of cold butter coated in flour melt in the oven and leave flaky pockets. Butter that warms and smears in makes the crust tough or greasy.

why.title: Just enough water
why.body: Water lets flour build gluten. Pastry wants only enough to hold together when squeezed; more makes it tough, and it shrinks in the oven.

why.title: A roux thickens
why.body: Flour cooked in butter for a couple of minutes loses its raw taste. Liquid whisked in slowly turns it into a smooth sauce that thickens as it simmers.

why.title: Why cut vents
why.body: The filling boils under the crust. Vents let the steam out so the crust stays crisp and doesn't puff up or split.

why.title: 165°F in the filling
why.body: The chicken was cooked first, then baked again under the crust. Reheated food is safe once the middle of the filling is back to 165°F.

wrong.fix: The liquid went in too fast. Whisk hard, or pour it through a strainer.
Simmer it 2 more minutes, stirring. It thickens as it cooks.
Bake 5 more minutes, until golden brown.
Bake it on a sheet pan next time to catch the drips.

choices: Flour cooked in butter, used to thicken a sauce

quiz.q: Why cut vents in the crust?
choices: To let steam out so the crust stays crisp
quiz.explain: Steam under the crust makes it soggy.

quiz.q: What temperature should the filling reach?

steps.text: Spread the crust's butter cubes on the plate and put them in the freezer. Put the water in a cup with a few ice cubes.
Whisk the crust's flour and salt in the large bowl. Add the cold butter and press it in with the back of the fork until the biggest pieces are the size of peas.
steps.look: Coarse crumbs, with pea-sized bits of butter.

steps.text: Sprinkle 3 tablespoons of the ice water over it and toss with the fork. Add more a tablespoon at a time until a squeezed handful holds.
Press the dough into a flat disk, cover it, and chill it.
Put a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 400°F.
Dice the onion, and slice the carrots and celery thin.
On the cutting board, cut the chicken into 1-inch pieces.
Wash the knife, the board, and your hands with hot, soapy water.
Melt 1 tablespoon of the filling's butter in the skillet over medium-high heat. Cook the chicken, stirring, until no pink is left.
Wash your hands and the spoon.
Check the biggest piece with the thermometer: 165°F. Move the chicken to a clean bowl.
Melt the other 4 tablespoons of butter in the skillet over medium heat. Cook the onion, carrots, and celery until soft.
Sprinkle in the ⅓ cup of flour and stir for 2 minutes.
steps.look: The vegetables are coated, with no dry flour.

steps.text: Slowly whisk in the broth, then the milk. Simmer, stirring, until thick.
steps.look: Thick enough to coat the back of the spoon.
steps.tip: Pour a little at a time, whisking, and it won't lump.

steps.text: Stir in the thyme, the filling's salt and pepper, the chicken, and the peas. Turn off the heat.
Roll the dough into an 11-inch circle. Lay it over the filling, tuck the edge in around the inside of the skillet, and cut 4 slits in the top.
Beat the egg with the tablespoon of water in the small bowl and brush it over the crust.
Wash your hands and the brush with soap, and throw away the rest of the egg wash.
Set the skillet on the sheet pan and bake until the crust is golden and the filling bubbles through the vents.
steps.look: Golden crust, with sauce bubbling at the slits.

steps.text: With oven mitts, pull out the rack. Push the thermometer through a slit into the middle of the filling: 165°F. If it's lower, bake 5 more minutes.
Turn off the oven. Set the skillet on the rack, lay an oven mitt over the handle, and let it rest before serving.
steps.tip: The handle stays hot a long time.

water.text: Add more ice water a tablespoon at a time until it just holds together. Don't break up the butter.

oven.text: Heat the oven to 400°F with a rack in the middle.

veg.text: Dice the onion, and slice the carrots and celery ¼ inch thick.

chicken.text: Trim the chicken of fat and cut it into 1-inch pieces on the raw-meat board.

wash-chicken.text: Wash the knife, board, and your hands.

brown.text: Brown the chicken in 1 tablespoon of the filling's butter in the skillet over medium-high heat until no pink is left.

wash-brown.text: Wash your hands and the spoon.

check-chicken.text: Check the largest pieces: 165°F. Move the chicken to a clean bowl.

soften.text: Soften the vegetables in the other 4 tablespoons of butter over medium heat.

roux.text: Stir in the ⅓ cup of flour and cook 2 minutes. Whisk in the broth, then the milk, a little at a time, and simmer until it coats a spoon.

finish.text: Stir in the thyme, salt, pepper, chicken, and peas, and turn off the heat.

top.text: Roll the rough puff ⅛ inch thick, a little wider than the skillet. Lay it over the filling, trim to a ½-inch overhang, and cut 4 vents.

egg-wash.text: Beat the egg with the water and brush the top, keeping the egg off the cut edges.
egg-wash.tip: Egg on the edges glues the layers shut.

wash-egg.text: Wash your hands and the brush, and discard the egg wash.

bake.text: Bake on the sheet pan until the top is puffed and deep golden.
bake.look: Tall, flaky, and deep golden, with sauce bubbling at the vents.

check.text: Check the filling through a vent: 165°F.

rest.text: Rest on the rack, a mitt over the handle, before serving.

add.text: Weigh 7 ounces of flour into the large bowl with the salt. Toss in the cold butter cubes so each is coated, then stir in ⅓ cup of ice water with the fork.
add.look: A shaggy dough with whole chunks of butter.

add.text: Pat the dough into a rectangle on a floured counter and roll it about 6 by 15 inches. Fold it in thirds like a letter, turn it a quarter turn, and roll and fold again.
add.tip: Brush off extra flour before each fold.

add.text: Roll and fold twice more, the same way.
add.look: Smooth, with streaks of butter but no butter showing through.

add.text: Wrap and chill until the filling is done.

move.title: A rough-puff lid
move.body: This week's skill is lamination. You'll make a rough puff: chunks of cold butter folded into dough four times until they're hundreds of thin layers, which puff tall and flaky over a chicken and vegetable filling thickened with a roux.

callback.body: The quiche's crust was cut in to pea size and rolled once. Rough puff starts with bigger chunks of butter and is folded four times, so it rises in layers instead of just flaking.

wrong.sign: Butter is breaking through the dough
wrong.fix: It's too warm. Dust the spot with flour, wrap it, and chill 15 minutes.

wrong.sign: The dough springs back when you roll
wrong.fix: The gluten is tight. Chill it 10 more minutes.
The butter melted into the dough before baking. Chill longer between folds next time.
The liquid went in too fast. Whisk hard, or pour it through a strainer.

quiz.q: How many layers of butter do four letter folds make?

choices: To keep the butter in sheets and relax the gluten
quiz.explain: Warm butter smears into the dough.

quiz.q: What makes rough puff rise in the oven?
What temperature should the filling reach under the crust?

add.title: Folding makes layers
add.body: Each letter fold triples the layers of butter and dough. Four folds give 81 layers of each. In the oven, the water in each butter layer turns to steam and lifts the dough above it.

add.title: Chill between folds
add.body: Rolling warms the butter and tightens the gluten. Fifteen minutes in the fridge after every two folds keeps the butter in sheets, not smears, and stops the dough fighting back.
